stem: The two main types of data, based on their source, are primary data and:
solution: Based on their source, data are of two main types: (1) primary data — data collected originally/first-hand by the investigator (or agency) themselves, directly from the source, for the specific purpose of their own enquiry; and (2) secondary data — data that have already been collected by someone else (some other person, agency, or organisation) for some other purpose, and which the investigator now uses (obtaining them from published or existing sources). So the distinction is about who originally collected the data and for what purpose. Understanding primary vs secondary data is a key prelims-relevant point. The two main types of data by source are primary data (collected first-hand by the investigator) and secondary data (already collected by others).

stem: Primary data are data that are:
options: collected originally (first-hand) by the investigator for their own specific purpose
solution: Primary data are data that are collected originally and directly (first-hand) by the investigator (or the agency conducting the enquiry) themselves, from the original source, specifically for the purpose of their own investigation/study. Because they are gathered directly for the purpose at hand, primary data are original, more reliable and relevant (fresh and fit for the specific purpose), but collecting them takes more time, money, and effort. (Examples: conducting a survey or interviews to gather the exact information you need.) Understanding primary data (original, first-hand data) is a prelims-relevant point. Primary data are collected originally (first-hand) by the investigator for their own specific purpose.

stem: Secondary data are data that:
options: have already been collected by someone else (for another purpose) and are used by the investigator
solution: Secondary data are data that have already been collected (in the past) by some other person, agency, or organisation — usually for some other purpose — and which the current investigator obtains and uses (from existing/published sources) for their own study. So secondary data are 'second-hand' data (not gathered by the user directly). Their advantage is that they are cheaper and quicker to obtain (already available); their disadvantage is that they may not exactly fit the investigator's purpose, and their accuracy/reliability depends on how well the original collector gathered them (so they must be used with care). (Examples: data from government publications, censuses, reports, journals.) Understanding secondary data is a prelims-relevant point. Secondary data have already been collected by someone else (for another purpose) and are used by the investigator.

stem: The methods of collecting PRIMARY data include personal interviews, mailed questionnaires, and:
options: telephone interviews (and direct observation, enumerator-collected schedules)
solution: The methods of collecting primary data (gathering original, first-hand information) include: (1) personal interviews — the investigator personally meets and asks the respondents; (2) mailed questionnaires — a questionnaire (list of questions) is mailed/sent to the respondents, who fill it in and send it back; (3) telephone interviews — asking the respondents over the phone; (4) collecting information through enumerators/schedules — trained enumerators (field workers) go to the respondents and fill in the schedules; and (5) direct personal observation. These are the various ways of obtaining primary data directly from the sources. (Secondary data, by contrast, are obtained from existing published/unpublished sources.) Understanding the methods of collecting primary data is a prelims-relevant point. Methods of collecting primary data include personal interviews, mailed questionnaires, telephone interviews, and enumerator-collected schedules/observation.

stem: A list of questions prepared and used to collect information from respondents is called a:
solution: A questionnaire is a list/set of questions, prepared systematically (in a logical order) on the subject of enquiry, which is used to collect information from the respondents. The respondents answer the questions (either by filling it in themselves — as with a mailed questionnaire — or by being asked the questions by an interviewer/enumerator). A well-designed questionnaire is very important for good data collection: the questions should be clear, simple, relevant, unambiguous, not too many, logically arranged, and not leading or embarrassing. The questionnaire is the main instrument/tool for collecting primary data in surveys. Understanding the questionnaire is a prelims-relevant point. A questionnaire is a list of questions used to collect information from respondents.

stem: A good questionnaire should have questions that are:
options: clear, simple, unambiguous, relevant, and not too many (and not leading or embarrassing)
solution: A good questionnaire should have questions that are: clear and simple (easy to understand); unambiguous (not confusing or open to different meanings); relevant (directly related to the purpose of the enquiry — no unnecessary questions); limited in number (not too long/many, to keep respondents willing to answer); logically arranged (in a sensible order); and not leading (not worded so as to suggest a particular answer) or embarrassing/personal (which respondents would not answer honestly). Designing the questionnaire well (with such good questions) is essential for collecting accurate, honest, and useful data. Understanding the features of a good questionnaire is a prelims-relevant point. A good questionnaire has clear, simple, unambiguous, relevant, and not-too-many questions, that are not leading or embarrassing.

stem: A statistical enquiry that collects data from EVERY unit/member of the whole population/group is called a:
solution: A census (or complete enumeration) is a method/enquiry in which data are collected from every single unit/member of the whole population (the entire group being studied) — no unit is left out. For example, the Census of India collects information from every household/person in the country. A census gives complete, accurate coverage of the whole population, but it is very costly, time-consuming, and laborious (especially for a large population). (This contrasts with a 'sample survey', which studies only a part of the population.) Understanding the census method (complete enumeration of all units) is a prelims-relevant point. A census (complete enumeration) collects data from every unit/member of the whole population.

stem: A method that collects data from only a PART (a representative selection) of the population, and uses it to draw conclusions about the whole, is called a:
solution: A sample survey (sampling method) is a method that collects data from only a part — a selected, representative portion (a 'sample') — of the whole population, and then uses the information from that sample to draw conclusions/make estimates about the entire population. For example, to estimate the average income of a city, one might survey a sample of, say, 1000 households (not all of them). Sampling is much cheaper, quicker, and easier than a full census, and if the sample is properly selected (representative), it can give quite accurate results. (This is contrasted with the census, which covers every unit.) Understanding the sample survey (studying a part to conclude about the whole) is a prelims-relevant point. A sample survey (sampling) collects data from only a representative part of the population and uses it to draw conclusions about the whole.

stem: The whole group about which information is to be collected/studied is called the:
solution: The population (also called the 'universe') is the entire group/collection of all the units (people, items, etc.) about which information is to be collected or which is to be studied in a statistical enquiry. For example, if we want to study the incomes of the households in a city, the 'population' is all the households in that city. A 'sample' is a part/subset selected from this population. So the population is the complete group of interest, and the sample is the smaller selected part of it that we actually study (in a sample survey). Understanding the population/universe (the whole group of study) is a prelims-relevant point. The population (universe) is the whole group about which information is to be collected/studied.

stem: A representative part of the population, selected for study in a survey, is called a:
solution: A sample is a part/subset — ideally a representative portion — of the population, that is selected and actually studied in a sample survey, in order to draw conclusions about the whole population. For the conclusions to be valid, the sample should be representative of the population (i.e., it should reflect the characteristics of the whole population fairly) and of adequate size. A properly selected sample allows the investigator to learn about the whole population by studying only a part of it (saving time, money, and effort compared to a full census). Understanding the sample (the studied part of the population) is a prelims-relevant point. A sample is a representative part of the population, selected for study in a survey.

stem: A major ADVANTAGE of the sample survey (over a census) is that it is:
options: less costly, quicker, and easier (needs fewer resources)
solution: A major advantage of the sample survey (over a full census/complete enumeration) is that it is less costly, quicker, and easier — because only a part of the population is studied (not every unit), it requires far less money, time, labour, and other resources than a census. This makes sampling feasible even when a census would be impractical (too big or expensive). Other advantages: sampling can allow more detailed and careful data collection (since fewer units are covered) and can even be more accurate in some ways (fewer units to handle means fewer errors). (Its main limitation is that, being based on a part, its results have some 'sampling error' and depend on the sample being properly selected/representative.) Understanding the advantages of sampling is a prelims-relevant point. A major advantage of the sample survey is that it is less costly, quicker, and easier than a census.

stem: For a sample to give reliable results, it must be __________ of the population.
solution: For a sample to give reliable, valid results (i.e., for the conclusions drawn from the sample to be true of the whole population), the sample must be representative of the population — meaning it should reflect/mirror the characteristics of the whole population fairly and accurately (it should be a good 'cross-section' of the population, not skewed toward any particular type). If the sample is not representative (is biased or unbalanced), then the conclusions drawn from it will be wrong/misleading (they will not apply to the whole population). Ensuring a representative sample (through proper selection methods, like random sampling, and adequate size) is therefore essential. Understanding that a sample must be representative is a prelims-relevant point. For reliable results, a sample must be representative of the population (reflecting its characteristics).

stem: The method of selecting a sample in which every unit of the population has an equal chance of being chosen (removing personal bias) is called __________ sampling.
solution: Random sampling is the method of selecting a sample in which every unit/member of the population has an equal (and independent) chance of being chosen for the sample. The selection is made purely by chance (e.g., by lottery, or using random numbers), NOT according to the investigator's personal choice or convenience. This removes personal bias from the selection, and it tends to give a representative sample (over which reliable statistical conclusions can be drawn). Random sampling is the most important and scientific method of sampling. (Other, non-random methods — like deliberate/purposive or convenience sampling — involve the investigator's choice and can introduce bias.) Understanding random sampling (equal chance, no bias) is a prelims-relevant point. Random sampling is where every unit of the population has an equal chance of being selected, removing personal bias.

stem: Errors that arise because a sample (only a part of the population) is studied instead of the whole population are called __________ errors.
solution: Sampling errors are the errors that arise simply because a sample (only a part of the population) is studied instead of the entire population — that is, because the sample, being just a part, may not perfectly represent the whole population, so the sample results may differ somewhat from the true population values. Sampling error is unavoidable in any sample survey (it exists because we study a part, not the whole), but it can be reduced by increasing the sample size and by proper (random) sampling methods. (Sampling errors occur only in sample surveys, not in a complete census — since a census studies the whole population.) Understanding sampling errors is a prelims-relevant point. Sampling errors arise because only a sample (part of the population), not the whole population, is studied.

stem: Errors that can occur in BOTH a census and a sample survey — due to mistakes in collecting, recording, or processing the data — are called __________ errors.
solution: Non-sampling errors are the errors that can occur in both a census (complete enumeration) and a sample survey — because they arise not from sampling, but from mistakes/faults in the actual process of collecting, recording, and processing the data. Examples include: errors in the collection of data (wrong questions, biased or careless enumerators, wrong or dishonest answers by respondents); errors in recording/entering the data; errors in the processing/tabulation and calculation; and errors due to incomplete coverage or non-response. Since these arise from the handling of the data (not from sampling), they can occur even in a full census. (In fact, a large census can have more non-sampling errors than a well-conducted sample survey, because of the sheer scale.) Understanding non-sampling errors is a prelims-relevant point. Non-sampling errors occur in both a census and a sample survey, due to mistakes in collecting, recording, or processing the data.

stem: An important government organisation in India that conducts large-scale sample surveys (on employment, consumption, etc.) is the:
solution: The National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) — now part of the National Statistical Office (NSO) — is the important government organisation in India that conducts large-scale sample surveys throughout the country on various socio-economic subjects, such as employment and unemployment, consumer expenditure (consumption), health, education, agriculture, and industry. These NSSO surveys are a major source of the sample-based statistical data used for economic planning and policy in India. (It complements the Census, which is a complete enumeration.) Understanding the NSSO (conductor of India's major sample surveys) is a prelims-relevant point. The National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) conducts large-scale sample surveys in India (on employment, consumption, etc.).

stem: The person who supplies/provides the information (answers the questions) in a survey is called the:
solution: The respondent is the person who supplies/provides the required information — i.e., who answers the questions — in a survey or enquiry. (The 'investigator' is the person conducting the enquiry/study; the 'enumerator' is the field worker who goes and collects the data from the respondents by asking the questions and recording the answers.) So the respondent is the source of the information (the one being surveyed/asked). The willingness and honesty of the respondents (and the clarity of the questions) greatly affect the quality of the data collected. Understanding who the respondent is is a prelims-relevant point. The respondent is the person who supplies the information (answers the questions) in a survey.

stem: A 'pilot survey' (a small trial survey conducted before the main survey) is useful because it:
options: helps test and improve the questionnaire and the survey plan (finding problems in advance)
solution: A pilot survey (or pretest) is a small-scale trial survey conducted on a small group before the main/full survey is carried out. It is useful because it helps to test and improve the questionnaire and the overall survey plan — by revealing, in advance, any problems or weaknesses: for example, questions that are unclear, confusing, ambiguous, or difficult to answer; missing questions; problems with the survey procedure or the enumerators' understanding; and estimates of the time, cost, and response likely. Based on the pilot survey, the questionnaire and plan can be corrected and improved before the main survey — ensuring that the main survey runs smoothly and collects good-quality data. Understanding the purpose of a pilot survey is a prelims-relevant point. A pilot survey is a small trial survey that helps test and improve the questionnaire and survey plan before the main survey.

stem: When choosing between a census and a sample survey, a census is generally preferred when:
options: the population is huge and resources are very limited
the population is small, or complete/very accurate coverage of every unit is essential
speed and low cost are the top priorities
only a rough estimate is needed
solution: A census (complete enumeration) is generally preferred over a sample survey when: the population is small (so covering every unit is feasible and not too costly); or when complete, exhaustive, and very accurate coverage of every single unit is essential (for example, a population census, where information about every person is needed, or where even small errors/omissions matter greatly). In such cases, the completeness and accuracy of the census justify its higher cost and effort. (Conversely, a sample survey is preferred when the population is very large, resources — time and money — are limited, speed is important, or only estimates/general conclusions are needed rather than complete individual coverage.) Understanding when a census is preferable is a prelims-relevant point. A census is preferred when the population is small, or when complete/very accurate coverage of every unit is essential.

stem: Assertion (A): Primary data are generally more reliable and suitable for a specific enquiry than secondary data. Reason (R): Primary data are collected first-hand, specifically for the purpose of that enquiry, whereas secondary data were collected by others for a different purpose. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that primary data are generally more reliable and more suitable/relevant for a specific enquiry than secondary data. And the reason is (R) that primary data are collected first-hand (directly by the investigator) specifically for the purpose of that particular enquiry — so they exactly fit the needs of the study, and the investigator controls and knows their accuracy and method; whereas secondary data were collected by someone else, for some other (different) purpose, so they may not exactly fit the current enquiry's needs (in terms of coverage, definitions, units, timing, etc.), and their reliability depends on how the original collector gathered them (which the current user may not fully know). So, because primary data are gathered directly for the specific purpose (R), they are more reliable and suitable for that enquiry (A) — R correctly explains A. (The trade-off is that primary data cost more time, money, and effort to collect.) Understanding this comparison is a prelims-relevant point. Primary data are more reliable/suitable for a specific enquiry because they are collected first-hand for that purpose, unlike secondary data collected by others for a different purpose.

stem: Sources of SECONDARY data include published sources (like government reports and journals) and __________ sources (like unpublished records of organisations).
solution: Secondary data can be obtained from two kinds of sources: (1) published sources — data that have been published and are publicly available, such as government publications and reports (censuses, surveys, official statistics), publications of international organisations (like the UN, World Bank, IMF), reports of committees and commissions, research journals, newspapers and magazines, and publications of trade associations and research institutions; and (2) unpublished sources — data that exist but have not been formally published, such as the records, files, and registers maintained by various organisations, government departments, companies, and researchers (available on request or through access). So secondary data come from both published and unpublished existing sources. Understanding the sources of secondary data is a prelims-relevant point. Secondary data come from published sources (government reports, journals, etc.) and unpublished sources (records of organisations).

stem: Before using secondary data, one should check their __________ (whether they are reliable, suitable for the purpose, and adequate).
solution: Before using secondary data, one must check/scrutinise them carefully — because they were collected by someone else for another purpose, so they may not be fit for the current use. In particular, one should check their: (1) reliability — whether the data are trustworthy/accurate (Who collected them? How? By what methods? Are they dependable?); (2) suitability — whether the data are suitable/relevant for the present purpose (Do they cover the right population, definitions, units, and time period for the current enquiry?); and (3) adequacy — whether the data are adequate/sufficient (in scope, coverage, and detail) for the purpose at hand. Only if the secondary data pass these tests (reliable, suitable, adequate) should they be used. This careful scrutiny is essential when using secondary data. Understanding these precautions (reliability, suitability, adequacy) is a prelims-relevant point. Before using secondary data, one should check their reliability, suitability, and adequacy for the purpose.

stem: The method of collecting primary data in which the investigator personally goes and collects the information directly from the sources is called __________ investigation.
solution: Direct personal investigation is the method of collecting primary data in which the investigator personally goes to the field and collects the required information directly (first-hand) from the sources/respondents (by personally meeting, observing, and questioning them). This method gives original, accurate, and reliable data (the investigator gets the information directly and can clarify doubts and observe), but it is costly, time-consuming, and laborious, and it is suitable mainly when the area/population is small and the enquiry needs great accuracy and depth. It is one of the several methods of collecting primary data. Understanding direct personal investigation is a prelims-relevant point. Direct personal investigation is where the investigator personally collects the information directly from the sources.

stem: In the method of collecting data through __________, the required information is filled in by trained field workers (enumerators) who ask the questions and record the answers.
solution: In the method of collecting data through enumerators (using schedules), trained field workers called enumerators go to the respondents, ask them the questions, and themselves fill in the answers on a form called a 'schedule'. This method is widely used for large enquiries (like the Census). Its advantages: it can cover a large area and even illiterate respondents (since the enumerator asks and records); the enumerator can explain/clarify questions, ensuring better and more complete responses; and the response rate is high. Its disadvantages: it is costly and requires training honest, capable enumerators (and biased or careless enumerators can introduce errors). (A 'schedule' is filled by the enumerator, whereas a 'questionnaire' is usually filled by the respondent themselves.) Understanding the enumerator/schedule method is a prelims-relevant point. In the enumerator/schedule method, trained field workers ask the questions and record the answers on a schedule.

stem: The key difference between a 'questionnaire' and a 'schedule' is that:
options: a questionnaire is usually filled in by the respondent themselves, while a schedule is filled in by the enumerator (who asks the questions)
a questionnaire is filled by the enumerator
solution: The key difference between a 'questionnaire' and a 'schedule' lies in who fills it in: a questionnaire is a list of questions that is usually given/sent to the respondents to fill in by themselves (they read and answer the questions on their own — as in a mailed questionnaire); whereas a schedule is a list of questions that is filled in by an enumerator (field worker), who asks the questions to the respondent and records the answers themselves. So both are lists of questions, but a questionnaire is respondent-filled (self-administered) and a schedule is enumerator-filled. (Because the enumerator fills the schedule, it can be used even with illiterate respondents and allows clarification.) Understanding the questionnaire-vs-schedule difference is a prelims-relevant point. A questionnaire is filled in by the respondent themselves, whereas a schedule is filled in by the enumerator who asks the questions.

stem: The mailed-questionnaire method has the advantage of being cheap and wide-reaching, but a major DISADVANTAGE is:
options: a low response rate (many people do not return it) and that only literate people can use it
solution: The mailed-questionnaire method (sending questionnaires by post/mail to respondents to fill in and return) has advantages — it is relatively cheap, and it can reach a wide/large and geographically scattered group of respondents. But it has major disadvantages: a low response rate (a large proportion of the mailed questionnaires are never returned, or are returned incomplete — because there is no one to encourage/help the respondents), which can make the data incomplete and unrepresentative; and it can only be used with literate respondents (who can read and fill in the form themselves), so it is unsuitable for illiterate populations. There is also no chance to clarify questions or verify the answers. These are important limitations of the mailed-questionnaire method. Understanding the disadvantages of the mailed-questionnaire method is a prelims-relevant point. The mailed-questionnaire method suffers from a low response rate and can be used only with literate respondents.

stem: In sampling, the LIST of all the units of the population (from which the sample is drawn) is called the:
solution: The sampling frame is the complete list of all the units/members of the population from which the sample is to be drawn/selected. For example, to draw a sample of households in a city, the sampling frame would be the list of all the households in that city. A good, complete, and accurate sampling frame is important for proper sampling — if the frame is incomplete or faulty (missing some units, or containing errors/duplicates), the sample drawn from it will be biased/unrepresentative, and the results unreliable. So the sampling frame is the base list from which the sample is selected. Understanding the sampling frame is a prelims-relevant point. The sampling frame is the list of all the units of the population from which the sample is drawn.

stem: A method of RANDOM sampling in which the units are numbered and the sample is selected using a lottery or a random number table is called __________ random sampling.
solution: Simple random sampling is the basic method of random sampling in which every unit of the population is given a number, and then the sample units are selected purely by chance — for example, by a lottery method (drawing numbered slips/tickets at random) or by using a random number table (or computer-generated random numbers). In simple random sampling, every unit has an equal and independent chance of being selected, and the selection is free from the investigator's bias. It is the simplest and most fundamental probability (random) sampling method. Understanding simple random sampling (lottery/random numbers) is a prelims-relevant point. Simple random sampling selects the sample by chance (using a lottery or random number table), giving every unit an equal chance.

stem: The sampling method in which the population is first divided into different groups (strata) — like age or income groups — and then a random sample is taken from each group, is called __________ sampling.
solution: Stratified sampling is the sampling method in which the population is first divided into different sub-groups or 'strata' — groups that are internally similar/homogeneous, based on some relevant characteristic (like age, income, gender, or region) — and then a (random) sample is drawn from each stratum (usually in proportion to its size). By ensuring that each important sub-group of the population is represented in the sample, stratified sampling gives a more representative and accurate sample (especially when the population is heterogeneous/varied) than simple random sampling. It is a widely-used, more refined sampling method. Understanding stratified sampling is a prelims-relevant point. In stratified sampling, the population is divided into groups (strata) and a random sample is taken from each group.

stem: Sampling methods in which the units are selected NOT by chance but by the investigator's choice or convenience (which can introduce bias) are called __________ sampling methods.
solution: Non-random (non-probability) sampling methods are those in which the sample units are selected NOT purely by chance, but according to the investigator's own choice, judgement, or convenience (so not every unit has a known/equal chance of selection). Examples include: purposive/deliberate sampling (the investigator deliberately picks certain units they think are representative or relevant); convenience sampling (picking whatever units are easily/conveniently available); and quota sampling (filling fixed quotas for different groups, but choosing the actual units by convenience). The drawback of non-random methods is that they can introduce the investigator's bias, so the sample may not be truly representative, and strict statistical (probability) conclusions cannot be validly drawn. (Random methods avoid this bias.) Understanding non-random sampling is a prelims-relevant point. Non-random (non-probability) sampling selects units by the investigator's choice or convenience (not by chance), which can introduce bias.

stem: In India, the Census (complete count of the population) is conducted by the office of the:
options: Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India
solution: In India, the Census — the decennial (every 10 years) complete enumeration of the entire population, along with the collection of demographic and socio-economic data — is conducted by the office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India (RGI), under the Ministry of Home Affairs. This office organises and carries out the massive nationwide census operation and compiles and publishes the results. The Census of India is one of the largest administrative and statistical exercises in the world, and a vital source of official data. Understanding who conducts India's Census (the RGI) is a prelims-relevant point. India's Census is conducted by the office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India (RGI).

stem: The first regular/synchronous Census of India was conducted in 1881, and it has been conducted __________ since then.
solution: The Census of India has been conducted regularly every ten years (decennially) — the first complete census was taken in 1872 (in parts), and the first synchronous (nationwide, on the same reference date) census was in 1881, and it has been conducted every ten years since then (in the years ending in '1' — 1891, 1901, ... 2011). This decennial census provides a regular, comprehensive count and profile of India's population every decade, which is invaluable for planning, policy, and research. Understanding that India's Census is decennial (every 10 years, since 1881) is a prelims-relevant point. India's Census has been conducted every ten years (decennially) since 1881.

stem: A 'leading question' (one worded so as to suggest or push the respondent toward a particular answer) should be __________ in a questionnaire.
solution: A 'leading question' — a question that is worded (framed) in such a way that it suggests, hints at, or pushes the respondent toward a particular (desired) answer (for example, 'Don't you agree that this policy is excellent?') — should be avoided in a questionnaire. Leading questions bias the responses (they influence the respondents to answer in a certain way, rather than giving their true/independent opinion), so the data collected become distorted and unreliable/misleading. To collect honest, unbiased data, questions should be neutral and objective (not leading). Avoiding leading questions is one of the principles of designing a good questionnaire. Understanding that leading questions should be avoided is a prelims-relevant point. Leading questions (which suggest a particular answer) should be avoided in a questionnaire, as they bias the responses.

stem: Questions that offer the respondent a fixed set of answer choices to pick from (like 'Yes/No' or multiple options) are called __________ questions.
solution: Closed-ended questions are questions that offer the respondent a fixed/limited set of answer choices to select from — such as 'Yes/No' questions, or multiple-choice questions with given options. The respondent simply picks one (or more) of the provided answers. Their advantages: the answers are easy to record, tabulate, and analyse (being standardised), and they are quicker to answer. Their disadvantage: they limit the respondent to the given choices (which may not capture their full/true view). (The opposite — 'open-ended' questions — let the respondent answer freely in their own words, capturing more detail but being harder to analyse.) Understanding closed-ended questions is a prelims-relevant point. Closed-ended questions offer the respondent a fixed set of answer choices to pick from (like Yes/No or multiple options).

stem: Questions that allow the respondent to answer freely in their own words (not limited to fixed choices) are called __________ questions.
solution: Open-ended questions are questions that allow the respondent to answer freely, in their own words, without being restricted to a fixed set of given choices (for example, 'What do you think about this policy?', where the respondent writes/says whatever they wish). Their advantage: they capture the respondent's full, detailed, and true views/opinions (rich, in-depth information not limited by preset options). Their disadvantage: the answers are varied and in the respondents' own words, making them harder to record, standardise, tabulate, and analyse. (The opposite — 'closed-ended' questions — restrict the answer to fixed choices, which are easier to analyse.) Understanding open-ended questions is a prelims-relevant point. Open-ended questions let the respondent answer freely in their own words, not limited to fixed choices.

stem: The precaution of keeping the questionnaire to a reasonable (not too long) length is important because:
options: a very long questionnaire tires and discourages respondents (leading to incomplete or careless answers, and non-response)
solution: Keeping the questionnaire to a reasonable (not too long) length is an important precaution, because a very long questionnaire tires, bores, and discourages the respondents — leading to problems such as: respondents refusing to answer or not returning it (non-response); or answering carelessly, hurriedly, or incompletely (especially toward the end) just to finish — which lowers the quality and completeness of the data. A questionnaire should therefore include only the necessary/relevant questions (no unnecessary ones) and be kept as short as the purpose allows, so that respondents are willing to answer all of it carefully and honestly. Understanding this precaution (reasonable length) is a prelims-relevant point. A questionnaire should not be too long, because a long one tires and discourages respondents, leading to incomplete or careless answers and non-response.

stem: The number of units included in a sample is called the:
solution: The sample size is the number of units (respondents/items) that are included in (selected for) the sample. Choosing an appropriate sample size is important: a larger sample size generally gives more reliable/accurate results (less sampling error) and is more representative, but it also costs more (in time, money, and effort); a very small sample may be cheap and quick but may be unreliable/unrepresentative (larger sampling error). So the sample size must be chosen to balance accuracy against cost — large enough to give reliable results, but not so large as to be wasteful. Understanding the sample size is a prelims-relevant point. The sample size is the number of units included in a sample.

stem: Generally, INCREASING the sample size (up to a point) tends to __________ the sampling error (making results more reliable).
solution: Generally, increasing the sample size (making the sample larger, up to a point) tends to reduce (decrease) the sampling error — that is, a larger sample is more likely to be representative of the population and to give results closer to the true population values (smaller error), making the results more reliable/accurate. This is because a bigger sample captures more of the population's variety and averages out the chance fluctuations. (However, beyond a certain point, the gain in accuracy from a bigger sample becomes small relative to the extra cost; and a huge sample also risks more non-sampling errors.) So, other things equal, a larger sample size reduces sampling error. Understanding the sample-size/sampling-error relationship is a prelims-relevant point. Increasing the sample size (up to a point) tends to reduce the sampling error, making the results more reliable.

stem: 'Non-response' in a survey (some selected respondents not answering) is a problem because it can make the collected data:
options: incomplete and possibly biased/unrepresentative (if the non-respondents differ from the respondents)
solution: 'Non-response' — when some of the selected respondents do not answer (they refuse, are not available, or do not return the questionnaire) — is a problem in a survey because it can make the collected data: incomplete (data are missing for those units); and, more seriously, possibly biased/unrepresentative — because the people who do NOT respond may differ systematically (in their characteristics or views) from those who do respond, so that the data from the respondents alone may not represent the whole population accurately (this is 'non-response bias'). For example, if busy or dissatisfied people are less likely to respond, the results will be skewed. High non-response thus undermines the reliability of the survey. (This is a form of non-sampling error.) Understanding the problem of non-response is a prelims-relevant point. Non-response can make survey data incomplete and biased/unrepresentative, if the non-respondents differ from the respondents.

stem: After the data are collected, they should be __________ (checked and corrected for errors, omissions, and inconsistencies) before analysis.
solution: After the data are collected, they should be edited/scrutinised — that is, carefully checked, verified, and corrected for errors, omissions, inconsistencies, and illegible or doubtful entries — before they are organised and analysed. This 'editing' of the raw data ensures that the data are as accurate, complete, and consistent as possible (removing or correcting mistakes made during collection/recording), so that the subsequent analysis and conclusions are reliable. Editing is an important step between the collection and the processing/analysis of data. (Careless data with uncorrected errors would lead to wrong conclusions.) Understanding the editing/scrutiny of collected data is a prelims-relevant point. Collected data should be edited/scrutinised (checked and corrected for errors, omissions, and inconsistencies) before analysis.

stem: In the method of collecting data through 'local correspondents' (or agents), information is supplied by:
options: local agents/correspondents who send in the information from their areas (as newspapers use local reporters)
solution: In the method of collecting data through 'local correspondents' (or agents), the information is supplied by local agents or correspondents appointed in different areas/localities, who collect the information from their respective areas (based on their local knowledge and observation) and send it in to the central investigator/office. This method is used, for example, by newspapers (which use local reporters/correspondents), and for regularly collecting data over a wide area at low cost. Its advantages: it is economical and useful for covering a wide area over time; its disadvantage: the data may be less accurate/reliable (as they depend on the correspondents' judgement, and different correspondents may vary), so it gives approximate results (suitable where a high degree of accuracy is not essential). Understanding the local-correspondents method is a prelims-relevant point. In the local-correspondents method, local agents send in information from their areas (as newspapers use local reporters).

stem: The method of 'indirect oral investigation' is used when:
options: the respondents can be directly asked
the required information cannot be obtained directly from the persons concerned, so it is gathered by questioning OTHER people (witnesses/third parties) who know about them
solution: The method of 'indirect oral investigation' is used when the required information cannot be obtained directly from the persons concerned themselves — for example, because they are unavailable, unwilling, or unable to give the information (or the matter is sensitive) — so instead, the information is gathered by questioning OTHER people (third parties/witnesses) who are connected with, or have knowledge about, the persons/matter being investigated (indirect sources). For instance, to enquire into someone's habits or an incident, one might question their neighbours, associates, or witnesses. This method is used by many enquiry committees and commissions. Its accuracy depends on how well-informed and unbiased the third parties are (so a number of persons are usually questioned). Understanding indirect oral investigation is a prelims-relevant point. Indirect oral investigation gathers information by questioning other people (third parties) who know about the persons/matter, when direct enquiry is not possible.

stem: Modern methods of conducting surveys (collecting primary data) now include __________ surveys, in addition to face-to-face and postal methods.
solution: Modern methods of conducting surveys (collecting primary data) now include online/internet surveys (using websites, email, apps, and online forms) and telephone/mobile-phone surveys, in addition to the traditional face-to-face (personal interview) and postal (mailed questionnaire) methods. These modern methods — enabled by computers, the internet, and mobile phones — can be faster, cheaper, and able to reach large, widely-scattered populations quickly. (However, they also have limitations — e.g., online/phone surveys reach only those with access to the internet/phones, which can bias the sample.) So technology has added new modes of data collection. Understanding these modern survey methods (online, telephone) is a prelims-relevant point. Modern survey methods include online/internet and telephone/mobile surveys, besides face-to-face and postal methods.

stem: The clear statement of the OBJECTIVE/purpose of the enquiry (what data are needed and why) should be decided:
options: before starting the data collection (at the very beginning)
solution: The clear statement of the objective/purpose of the enquiry — deciding exactly what data are needed and why (the aim of the study) — should be decided before starting the data collection, at the very beginning of the statistical enquiry. This is essential, because the objective guides every subsequent step: it determines what data to collect, from whom, by what method (primary/secondary, census/sample), in what detail, and how to design the questionnaire. Without a clear, pre-decided objective, the data collected may be irrelevant, incomplete, or unusable for the intended purpose. So defining the objective clearly at the outset is the crucial first step of planning a statistical enquiry. Understanding this (objective decided before collection) is a prelims-relevant point. The objective/purpose of the enquiry should be clearly decided before starting the data collection.

stem: A key ADVANTAGE of a census over a sample survey is that it:
options: covers every unit, giving complete and detailed information about the whole population (no sampling error)
solution: A key advantage of a census (complete enumeration) over a sample survey is that it covers every single unit of the population, giving complete, detailed, and comprehensive information about the whole population — with no sampling error (since the whole population is studied, not just a sample, there is no error from sampling). This makes the census results complete and (in principle) fully representative, and it provides information down to the smallest level (every area/group). (Its disadvantages, compared to sampling, are its much greater cost, time, and effort, and the risk of larger non-sampling errors due to the huge scale.) Understanding the advantage of a census (complete coverage, no sampling error) is a prelims-relevant point. A key advantage of a census is that it covers every unit, giving complete, detailed information about the whole population, with no sampling error.

stem: The choice of the method of data collection depends on factors such as the purpose, the __________, the resources (time and money) available, and the required accuracy.
solution: The choice of the method of data collection (primary vs secondary; census vs sample; and the particular technique — interview, questionnaire, enumerator, etc.) depends on several factors, including: the purpose/objective of the enquiry (what is needed and why); the nature and size of the population/enquiry (small or large, homogeneous or varied, literate or illiterate, scattered or concentrated); the resources available — the time and money (budget) at hand; and the degree of accuracy required (whether complete precision or an approximate estimate is needed). Weighing these factors, the investigator chooses the most suitable and feasible method for the situation. So the method is chosen to fit the purpose, the population, the resources, and the accuracy needed. Understanding the factors affecting the choice of method is a prelims-relevant point. The choice of data-collection method depends on the purpose, the nature/size of the population, the resources available, and the required accuracy.

stem: Which is an example of SECONDARY data?
options: Data you collect by personally interviewing shopkeepers today
Population figures you take from a published Census of India report
Observations you record yourself in a field study
solution: Of the options, 'population figures you take from a published Census of India report' is an example of secondary data — because these data were collected earlier by someone else (the Census organisation) for its own purpose, and you are now using them (from the published source) for your study. The other options are all examples of primary data (data you collect first-hand yourself): personally interviewing shopkeepers, conducting your own survey, and recording your own observations in a field study — in each case, you gather the data directly for your own purpose. So the key is whether the data are collected by you first-hand (primary) or taken from an existing source collected by others (secondary). Understanding how to identify secondary data (with an example) is a prelims-relevant point. Population figures taken from a published Census report are secondary data (collected by others), unlike data you collect first-hand yourself (primary).

stem: The sampling method in which units are selected at regular intervals from a list (e.g., every 10th name) is called __________ sampling.
solution: Systematic sampling is the sampling method in which the units are selected from a list (the sampling frame) at regular, fixed intervals — after choosing a random starting point, every 'kth' unit is selected (for example, every 10th name on the list). So if you want a sample of 100 from a list of 1000, you would take every 10th unit (starting from a randomly chosen one among the first 10). Systematic sampling is simple and convenient to use (easier than pure random selection from a large list), and it usually gives a fairly representative sample — as long as the list is not arranged in a pattern that coincides with the sampling interval (which could bias it). It is a commonly used sampling method. Understanding systematic sampling is a prelims-relevant point. Systematic sampling selects units at regular intervals from a list (e.g., every 10th unit, after a random start).

stem: Assertion (A): A sample survey can sometimes give more accurate results than a census. Reason (R): With fewer units to handle, a sample survey can be conducted more carefully (with better-trained staff and closer supervision), reducing non-sampling errors. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that a sample survey can sometimes give more accurate results than a census. And the reason is (R) that, because a sample survey has far fewer units to handle than a census, it can be conducted more carefully and thoroughly — with better-trained and better-supervised staff, more careful and detailed data collection, and closer checking — which reduces the non-sampling errors (the errors of collection, recording, and processing). A huge census, by contrast, involves an enormous number of units and staff, which can lead to many non-sampling errors (careless work, mistakes) despite its complete coverage. So, although a sample has sampling error, its lower non-sampling error (from being done more carefully) can make it overall more accurate than a sprawling census — R correctly explains A. Understanding this (a careful sample can beat a sprawling census) is a prelims-relevant point. A sample survey can be more accurate than a census because, with fewer units, it can be conducted more carefully, reducing non-sampling errors.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Collection of Data' is that:
options: The collection of data is the crucial first step of any statistical study, and it must be done carefully — choosing between primary data (collected first-hand, by methods like interviews and questionnaires) and secondary data (already collected by others), and between a census (covering every unit) and a sample survey (studying a representative part) — because the quality and reliability of all later analysis depends on how well the data are collected
Only secondary data should ever be used
solution: The chapter conveys that the collection of data is the crucial first step (foundation) of any statistical study — since the quality, accuracy, and reliability of all the later stages (organisation, presentation, analysis, and interpretation) and of the final conclusions depend entirely on how well the data are collected ('garbage in, garbage out'). It explains the two main types of data by source: primary data — collected originally/first-hand by the investigator, directly for the specific purpose of their own enquiry (by methods such as personal interviews, mailed questionnaires, telephone interviews, and enumerators/schedules, using a well-designed questionnaire) — which are more reliable and relevant but costlier and slower to collect; and secondary data — already collected by someone else for another purpose, and obtained from existing sources — which are cheaper and quicker but must be used with care (as they may not exactly fit the purpose, and their reliability depends on the original collector). It also explains the two methods of collecting primary data in terms of coverage: the census (complete enumeration), which collects data from every unit of the population (giving complete coverage, but very costly and time-consuming — preferred when the population is small or complete accuracy is essential); and the sample survey (sampling), which studies only a representative part (sample) of the population and uses it to draw conclusions about the whole (cheaper, quicker, and easier — preferred for large populations or limited resources), where the sample must be representative (ideally selected by random sampling to avoid bias). And it distinguishes sampling errors (arising from studying only a sample) from non-sampling errors (mistakes in collecting/recording/processing, which can occur even in a census). Throughout, the emphasis is on collecting data carefully, systematically, and appropriately (choosing the right type and method for the purpose), so that the data are reliable and fit for use. Understanding the sources, types, and methods of data collection — and the need to do it carefully — is the central concern of this chapter. The collection of data is the crucial first step of any statistical study, requiring careful choices between primary and secondary data, and between a census and a sample survey — because all later analysis depends on how well the data are collected.
